content: To get us started, in plain language, what does Harvest Ready Meals do or plan to do for its customers day-to-day?

We are a Ready-to-Eat Food Producer with two lines of business: retail packaged meals for grocery chains and bulk meal kits for institutional cafeterias. Retail has two product lines (vegan and keto trays), and bulk has two products (50-serving trays and 200-serving trays).

Harvest Ready Meals is a food production business that prepares and packages ready-to-eat meals in a commercial facility, selling them as branded retail trays (vegan and keto) to grocery chains and as bulk meal kits (50-serving and 200-serving trays) to institutional cafeterias; revenue comes from per-tray sales to these business customers rather than direct-to-consumer or on-site dining. It operates as a refrigerated/ready-to-heat product manufacturer and distributor, not a restaurant, caterer, or meal-delivery service to individual households. Does that description match what you have in mind?
On-site production with refrigerated distribution to customer loading docks.

Thanks, that’s helpful context. Let me refine the description and you can confirm: Harvest Ready Meals is a ready-to-eat food manufacturer that produces meals on-site in a commercial facility and distributes them via refrigerated transport to business customers’ loading docks, selling branded vegan and keto retail trays to grocery chains and bulk 50-serving and 200-serving trays to institutional cafeterias; it operates as a chilled food production and distribution business, not a restaurant, retail store, or direct-to-consumer meal delivery service. Does that fully capture what the business is?  

Based on the start date you provided, I'm treating this as pre-revenue for planning context. If that's off, tell me and I'll adjust.
yes

Understood. To keep terminology simple going forward, would you describe Harvest Ready Meals as primarily selling to businesses (grocery chains and institutions), rather than directly to individual consumers?
yes

Got it, so this is a business-to-business operation. Next, since you mentioned two lines of business (retail trays for groceries and bulk trays for institutions), do you want us to track these as two separate operational lines (retail vs. bulk), each with its own products and capacity, or keep everything combined as one overall operation?
yes

Great, we’ll treat this as two separate lines: Retail (vegan and keto trays) and Bulk (50-serving and 200-serving trays). I’ll start with the Retail side and then move to Bulk. For the Retail line, what should we consider as the basic “unit” for planning and pricing: one individual packaged tray (e.g., a single vegan or keto meal tray) sold to the grocery customer?
Two lines: retail meal trays (vegan and keto) and bulk meal kits (50-serving and 200-serving trays).

Understood on the two lines: retail meal trays (vegan and keto) and bulk meal kits (50-serving and 200-serving trays of meals for cafeterias). For the retail line, can we define the basic unit as one individual packaged meal tray (either vegan or keto) sold to a grocery customer?
yes

Great. Let’s treat the retail line as having two products, each with the unit defined as one individual packaged tray. First, focusing just on the vegan retail trays: in a fully booked week once you’re up and running, about how many vegan trays do you expect you can produce and have ready to ship?
Two lines: retail meal trays (vegan and keto) and bulk meal kits (50-serving and 200-serving trays).

Got it, we’ll keep it clearly structured as two lines: retail meal trays (vegan and keto) and bulk meal kits (50-serving and 200-serving trays). Let’s start with one product and go step by step. 

Focusing first on the vegan retail meal tray: in a fully booked week once you’re operating, about how many individual vegan trays do you expect you can produce and have ready to ship?
1500 retail trays and 40 bulk trays per week.

Thanks, that’s clear. I’ll interpret that as total weekly capacity across all products: 1,500 retail meal trays (vegan + keto combined) and 40 bulk trays (mix of 50-serving and 200-serving) in a fully booked week. Does that match your intent?
yes
Perfect. For the retail side, let’s split that 1,500-tray weekly capacity: roughly how many of those 1,500 do you expect to be vegan vs. keto in a typical fully booked week?
Retail is one packaged meal tray; bulk is one prepared tray of 50 or 200 servings.

Understood on the unit definitions: for retail, one unit is a single packaged meal tray; for bulk, one unit is one prepared tray (either 50-serving or 200-serving). For planning, how do you want to allocate your 1,500 weekly retail tray capacity between vegan and keto trays (for example, mostly vegan, mostly keto, or roughly 50/50)?
yes

I’ll assume, unless you prefer otherwise, that the 1,500 weekly retail tray capacity is split roughly 50/50 between vegan and keto (about 750 vegan trays and 750 keto trays) for planning. Is that a reasonable starting point, or would you like a different split between vegan and keto?
yes

Great, we’ll use 750 vegan trays and 750 keto trays per week as your retail capacity, and 40 bulk trays per week total across the 50-serving and 200-serving formats. Next, for the retail line, what is your target average wholesale price per tray to grocery customers for the vegan and keto products (either one price for both, or two separate prices)?
8 per retail tray, 350 per 50-serving tray, 1200 per 200-serving tray.

Perfect, so we’ll use $8 per retail tray, $350 per 50-serving bulk tray, and $1,200 per 200-serving bulk tray as your agreed prices. To confirm the bulk side: out of your total capacity of 40 bulk trays per week, how many do you expect to be 50-serving trays versus 200-serving trays in a typical fully booked week?
yes

I’ll assume, for planning, that your 40 bulk trays per week are split 50/50 between formats, so about 20 of the 50-serving trays and 20 of the 200-serving trays in a fully booked week. Does that split work for you, or do you want a different mix between 50-serving and 200-serving trays?
yes

{{fact:business.name}} operates as a B2B ready-to-eat food producer with two distinct lines of business: (1) retail packaged meal trays (vegan and keto) for grocery chains and (2) bulk meal kits in 50-serving and 200-serving prepared trays for institutional cafeterias. Production is done on-site in a commercial kitchen/food production facility, with meals prepared, packed, and held under refrigeration according to standard food safety protocols. Finished units ({{fact:ops.unit_name}} at the line/product level) are shipped via refrigerated distribution and delivered directly to customers’ loading docks on scheduled order cycles, with typical lead times assumed to be a few days from order confirmation to delivery once accounts and menus are set. Capacity in a fully booked week is primarily constrained by labor and kitchen/packaging line throughput rather than by demand or systems, so planning focuses on staffing and production scheduling to reach {{fact:ops.units_per_week_capacity}} units per week at agreed pricing around {{fact:ops.unit_price}} per unit at the product level. Standard food manufacturing licensing, health department permits, and food safety/FSMA compliance appropriate to a {{fact:ops.legal_entity}} operating a ready-to-eat food production facility are assumed to be incorporated into day-to-day operations; exact requirements, including any USDA/FDA, state, and local approvals, vary by jurisdiction and will be finalized with local regulators and insurers before production start.

Now, based on your model (a ready-to-eat food production facility serving grocery chains and institutional cafeterias), here are additional roles that are typically important to have covered over time. These are not hiring instructions—just a planning view of role coverage; wage estimates would be handled separately:

1) Owner / General Manager  
Reason: Overall P&L responsibility, contracts with grocery chains and institutions, banking, insurance, and coordination of permitting and food manufacturing licenses. In a sole proprietor setup, this is often the founder wearing multiple hats, including basic HR and vendor management.

2) Food Safety & Quality Assurance Lead  
Reason: Designs and maintains food safety plans (HACCP/FSMA), coordinates with health departments and any USDA/FDA requirements, oversees recall procedures, labeling compliance, shelf-life validation, and routine quality checks across both retail and bulk product lines.

3) Production Supervisors / Line Leads  
Reason: Support the Plant Manager by running specific shifts or lines (e.g., retail trays vs. bulk trays), enforcing SOPs on the floor, managing daily labor assignments, and making sure scheduled capacity is met without compromising safety or consistency.

4) Sales & Account Manager (B2B)  
Reason: Owns relationships with grocery category managers and institutional food service directors, manages pricing discussions, coordinates tastings and samples, and handles the sales pipeline and reorders. This role is usually the main external face of the business.

5) Logistics & Inventory Coordinator  
Reason: Oversees inbound ingredients, refrigerated storage, and outbound shipping; manages relationships with refrigerated trucking providers, ensures orders are staged and loaded correctly for on-time delivery, and tracks inventory for both ingredients and finished goods.

6) Administrative / Bookkeeping Support  
Reason: Handles invoicing, basic bookkeeping, payroll coordination, and support for compliance documentation and insurance. This can be part-time or outsourced early on but is important for clean financial records and support with lender/insurer requests.

These can be combined in the early stages (for example, the owner also acting as Sales & Account Manager, or the Plant Manager also handling some food-safety admin), then split into distinct positions as volume grows.
